messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Whassup with this simple bivariate normal model that's so damn slow and also throws weird exceptions?
parts:
Hi, attached is Stan and R code for a bivariate normal model with rounding error. When I run it with a mere 1000 data points it takes forever (5 minutes for two of the chains, the other third chain took 10 minutes!, and the fourth chain was still running after 15 minutes so I said fuckit and did control-C!). Why is it so damn slow???

Also, I get these weird warnings:

The following numerical problems occured the indicated number of times on chain 3
count
Exception thrown at line 17: multi_normal_log: Covariance matrix is not symmetric. Covariance matrix 12
Exception thrown at line 17: multi_normal_log: LDLT_Factor of covariance parameter is not positive d 1

--

I can't figure this out: I've actually declared Sigma as a covariance matrix, so shouldn't it automatically be symmetric? This is weird.

I was curious so I re-ran the model, specifying mu and Sigma as data. (I look forward to the day when we can run Stan with certain parameters set to fixed values, instead of having to write multiple Stan programs to do this.) Stan was still slow.

A

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Whassup with this simple bivariate normal model that's so damn slow and also throws weird exceptions?
parts:
I don't know why it'd be slow with fixed Sigma.

With variable Sigma, you should be using Cholesky factors,
or ideally, Cholesky factors of correlation matrices
with LKJ priors.

The rounding errors may be running off to -0.5 or + 0.5, forcing
the unconstrained parameters try to run off to + or - infinity.

I understand that you are assuming that the measurmeent is accurate
to +/- 0.5, but maybe loosening this assumption can help.

Too bad we don't have enough distributed functions to remove
the need for that loop.

I thought we'd squashed that symmetry bug. But then this
model has problems that may make the symmetry a side-effect.

- Bob

I find that so confusing! But I guess there's no way to simplify it in Stan so it looks to the user like a covariance matrix but is actually Cholesky under the hood?

> The rounding errors may be running off to -0.5 or + 0.5, forcing
> the unconstrained parameters try to run off to + or - infinity.
>
> I understand that you are assuming that the measurmeent is accurate
> to +/- 0.5, but maybe loosening this assumption can help.

It's not a matter of "accurate to +/- 0.5"; the assumption is that the continuous numbers are being rounded. For example, heights being recorded to the nearest inch. But, sure, in practice there's continuous measurement error too: "66 inches" is not really "65.5 to 66.5 inches," it's really "65.5 to 66.5 inches + error."

>
> Too bad we don't have enough distributed functions to remove
> the need for that loop.
>
> I thought we'd squashed that symmetry bug. But then this
> model has problems that may make the symmetry a side-effect.

I have no idea, just thought I'd share it. I remain surprised that such a simple model took so long to run, even with fixed hyperparamters so that all it's doing is moving in the latent space of the measurement errors.

Just for laffs I can try re-running the model with Gaussian errors and see if that runs much faster.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Whassup with this simple bivariate normal model that's so damn slow and also throws weird exceptions?
parts:
1000 data points but also 2 parameters per data point for 2000 total parameters.
Try fitting that many parameters in BUGS in three minutes!

Using the fixed hyperparameters I ran 4 chains and 3 ran really quickly but one 
stalled and took about ten times as long as the rest.  The adaptation wasn’t off
for that chain, so it looks like it ended up getting stuck in an awkward region of
parameter space.

Looking at the energy diagnostic it looks like the posterior is might be heavy-tailed.
This is consistent with the performance variation — one chain could get stuck in
the tails and require very, very long trajectories to get back.  That motivates looking
at the treedepth/n_leapfrog…and indeed the slow chain did have _much_ longer 
trajectories!  In three fast chains averaged around 15 leapfrog steps per transition 
while the slow chain was saturating at the default threshold of 1023.  

I didn’t see any obvious heavy-tailed behavior in the sample histograms, but I also 
didn’t split anything up by chain.  

The data clearly aren't informing the rounding error parameters at all (all of their 
marginal histograms are uniform from -0.5 to 0.5) and this means that the posterior 
density on the unconstrained scale is just the lower/upper bound Jacobian. If that
Jacobian looks heavy-tailed then we’d have the source of our problem.

Looks like those diagnostics really are useful...

but it shouldn’t be so heavy-tailed to cause serious fitting issues. Moving
to the probit might make the posterior slightly more well-behaved.

and, as Bob noted, you’re trying to sample too close to the boundaries
at -0.5 and 0.5.

A covariance matrix is actually Cholesky under the hood. It's
just that pulling it back to a covariance matrix and applying
the Jacobian is arithmetically imprecise. And then it just needs
to be factored again inside the multi-normal desnity.

>> The rounding errors may be running off to -0.5 or + 0.5, forcing
>> the unconstrained parameters try to run off to + or - infinity.
>>
>> I understand that you are assuming that the measurmeent is accurate
>> to +/- 0.5, but maybe loosening this assumption can help.

I got that, but that's the only error you're assuming, right?

> For example, heights being recorded to the nearest inch. But, sure, in practice there's continuous measurement error too: "66 inches" is not really "65.5 to 66.5 inches," it's really "65.5 to 66.5 inches + error."

Isn't the continuous measurement error inside the rounding? My point
was just that this will try to drive a value up against a hard boundary
if it really wants to be closer to the expected value.

- Bob

with

but that'll be a lot slower.

Ben added Phi_approx, but I think that's just a scaled inverse logit.
